headline: Bay water pushing 78 degrees sends the fluke running for the inlet
subhead: New moon springs load up the Marine Parkway rip while bluefish crash bunker in the Rockaway wash.
body_markdown:
Last week the bay did what it does every July when we get a stretch of sun and light wind — it cooked. I was seeing 78 and change on my temp gauge in the back channels off Grassy Bay by Thursday, and that's too warm for fluke to sit comfortably on the flats where they were feeding in May and June. They didn't disappear, they just packed up and moved to where the water still moves and stays cooler — the deeper channels, the Beach Channel drop, and out through Rockaway Inlet itself. That's the story of the whole bay right now: warm, mostly slack, green water inside, and a cleaner, cooler push wherever the tide is actually working. The moon's swinging toward new on the 10th, which means we're building into spring tides through the weekend — bigger swings, stronger current, and that's exactly the medicine this bay needs right now to flush some of that heat and get bait moving again.

Wind's been out of the south and southwest most days, which keeps the ocean side a little bumpy but doesn't hurt the bay much — if anything it's helped push a little cooler water in through the inlet on the bigger tides. With the new moon spring tides peaking Friday through Monday, look for the flood to run harder and longer at Marine Parkway Bridge, and the outgoing to really rip through the inlet by the channel markers off Breezy. That's the window I'm circling. Stronger current means bait gets pinned against structure instead of drifting lazy, and that's when the bigger bass and the blues decide it's worth their while to show up and eat instead of just cruising.

Fluke fishing in the bay proper has gone from good to patchy — guys who were limiting out in May on the flats off Ruffle Bar and Big Egg Marsh are working a lot harder for fewer fish now that the water's warm and slack. The move has been out toward the inlet and the deeper cuts. I had a solid afternoon last week working the drop-off just inside Breezy Point in about 18 to 22 feet, dragging a 5-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a 3/4-ounce bucktail nice and slow on the last two hours of the outgoing. Picked up three keepers and lost a good one at the boat that felt bigger than the 12-pound doormat that got weighed in over on the Jersey side a couple weeks back — that fish is still the one everybody's talking about at the shops, and it's a reminder that the big girls are out there if you put the right bait in the right depth. If you're fishing from a kayak or small boat, don't waste your time on the shallow bay flats right now — head for Beach Channel or work the edges where the current still runs, even at low water.

Stripers are where the new moon tide is going to matter most. Marine Parkway Bridge has been staging fish on the outgoing all week, and with the bigger spring tides coming in through the weekend, I expect that bite to sharpen up. Live eels drifted through the pilings on the last two hours of the outgoing have been the ticket, along with bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig for the fish holding deeper in the current seam. Nothing enormous yet — mostly schoolies to mid-20-inchers — but the current's about to get a lot more serious, and stronger flow usually means the better fish start showing up to work the rip instead of just the small ones. I'd be at that bridge on the Friday through Sunday outgoing this week, right as the tide starts really moving, and I'd stay through the last hour before dead low.

Bluefish have been the most reliable thing in the surf. Rockaway Beach has had real bunker schools pushing through close to the beach in the mornings, and when the blues find them it's fast and violent — poppers and metal like a Kastmaster or an Ava jig worked at speed have been drawing crashing strikes right in the wash from Beach 90th down toward Beach 116th. It's not an all-day thing — it's short windows, usually first light and again right before dark, so don't sleep in if you want in on it. Porgies are still a solid, honest bite for anyone fishing bottom rigs with sandworms or clam off Cross Bay Bridge and in the Beach Channel — nothing glamorous, but steady, and a good option for family trips off Canarsie Pier where the kids can get bit without much fuss.

Weakfish, I'll be straight with you — despite the warm water, I'm still not hearing real reports out of the bay or inlet. The water's plenty warm enough on paper, but warm water alone hasn't been enough to trigger them the last couple seasons, and this year's no different so far. I wouldn't plan a trip around them yet.

Looking ahead, the new moon spring tides building through the weekend are the story. If the current comes on as strong as it should at Marine Parkway and the inlet, I'd fish the outgoing there over the next four or five days before anything else — that's where the stripers and the bigger blues are going to concentrate. Plan B if that bridge bite doesn't materialize: work the Breezy Point drop-off on the last of the outgoing for fluke, because that pattern's been consistent even while everything else in the bay sorts itself out.
